chunks.title: Macula anatomy, RPE & Bruch
chunks.tldr: Macula ~5–6 mm (central 15–20°). Fovea 1.5 mm (≈ disc), foveola 0.35 mm (cones only, no ganglion cells), FAZ ~0.6 mm. RPE = outer blood–retinal barrier. Bruch = 5 layers.
points: Macula has >1 layer of ganglion cells. Yellow lutein and zeaxanthin (macula lutea).
Fovea: 1.5 mm pit. Foveola: 0.35 mm floor, thinnest retina, densely packed cones + Müller cells. Umbo: centre, foveolar reflex (lost early in disease).
FAZ: no capillaries, ~0.6 mm, measured accurately on FA.
RPE: single hexagonal layer; apical melanosomes; taller and more pigmented at the fovea.
RPE jobs: tight junctions = outer BRB, pumps water out of the subretinal space, keeps retina attached, phagocytoses outer segments, vitamin A cycle, absorbs stray light, transports nutrients/waste.
Bruch membrane (5 layers): RPE basement membrane, inner collagen, elastic, outer collagen, choriocapillaris basement membrane. Damage → CNV.
chunks.hook: Fovea ≈ disc size (1.5 mm). Foveola ≈ ¼ of that.

cards.q: Diameter of the foveola?
cards.a: About 0.35 mm.

cards.q: What forms the outer blood–retinal barrier?
cards.a: RPE cells and their tight junctions (zonulae occludentes).

chunks.title: Macular symptoms
chunks.tldr: Macula = positive scotoma (something in the way) + metamorphopsia. Optic nerve = negative scotoma (missing patch) + early colour loss.
points: Blurred near vision first.
Positive scotoma: a dark blob blocking the centre.
Metamorphopsia: distorted lines (Amsler) → not optic neuropathy.
Micropsia: cones spread apart (e.g. oedema). Macropsia: cones bunched (e.g. ERM traction).
Colour less affected than in optic neuropathy.
Dark adaptation trouble, lingering after-images.
chunks.hook: Micro = cones spread (fluid). Macro = cones squeezed (membrane).

cards.q: Micropsia results from what at the fovea?
cards.a: Spreading apart of foveal cones (e.g. subretinal fluid).

chunks.title: Fluorescein angiography: basics & phases
chunks.tldr: Fluorescein: excite 490 nm (blue) → emits 530 nm (yellow-green). Phases: choroidal (9–15 s) → arterial → AV (laminar) → venous → late. Fovea is dark (FAZ, xanthophyll, dense RPE).
points: ~70% protein-bound. Excreted in urine over 24–36 h.
Choriocapillaris leaks free fluorescein; RPE tight junctions block it (outer BRB). Retinal capillary endothelium blocks bound + free (inner BRB).
Filters: cobalt blue excitation, yellow-green barrier.
Contraindications: fluorescein allergy; relative: severe allergy history, renal failure (lower dose), pregnancy, asthma, heart disease. Shellfish/iodine allergy is not a contraindication.
Side effects: yellow skin/urine (always), extravasation pain, nausea, itch, vasovagal, anaphylaxis ~1:2000, death ~1:220,000. Have resuscitation ready.
5 ml of 10% IV over 5–10 s (or oral 30 mg/kg).

Choroidal (pre-arterial) 9–15 s: patchy choroid + cilioretinal artery. Arterial: ~1 s later. AV/capillary: laminar venous flow. Venous: full venous filling; perifoveal capillaries peak 20–25 s. Late: fading, disc stains; gone from vessels ~10 min.
Dark fovea: no vessels (FAZ), xanthophyll, dense melanin/lipofuscin RPE.
chunks.hook: FA phases: Choroid → Arteries → Laminar veins → Full veins → Late ('C A L F L').

cards.q: Which FA phase shows laminar venous flow?
cards.a: Arteriovenous (capillary) / early venous phase.

cards.q: Excitation and emission wavelengths of fluorescein?
cards.a: ~490 nm excitation, ~530 nm emission.

chunks.title: Reading FA: hyper vs hypo
chunks.tldr: Hyper: window defect (early, same size, fades), pooling (in a space), leakage (grows in size + brightness), staining (late). Hypo: blocking or filling defect.
points: Autofluorescence (before dye): disc drusen, astrocytic hamartoma. Pseudofluorescence: filter overlap.
Window defect: RPE atrophy (GA, macular hole, RPE tear) → early bright, stays the same size, fades with the choroid.
Pooling: dye collecting in a space. Subretinal (CSR: grows slowly, well-defined) or sub-RPE (PED: brighter but same size).
Leakage: grows in size and intensity → broken inner BRB (DR, RVO, CMO, papilloedema) or vessels without tight junctions (CNV, NV, tumours, Coats).
Staining: late retention (drusen, scars, sclera, normal disc).
Blocking: preretinal blood blocks everything; deeper blood/exudate/pigment/CHRPE/naevus blocks choroid but retinal vessels still show.
Filling defect: occlusion (arteries, veins, capillary dropout, AION) or loss of vessels (myopia, choroideremia).
Read systematically: clinical info → which eye → colour/red-free/AF → transit time → quick scan for key signs (lacy CNV, smokestack) → detailed description.
chunks.hook: Window = same shape. Leak = spreading puddle.

cards.q: Early hyperfluorescence that fades without changing size?
cards.a: Window defect (RPE atrophy).

cards.q: Hyperfluorescence increasing in brightness but not size?
cards.a: Pooling in a sub-RPE space (PED).

chunks.title: ICGA
chunks.tldr: Infrared (805/835 nm) sees through RPE, xanthophyll, thin blood → images the choroid. ~98% protein-bound so stays in choroidal vessels. Best for PCV, RAP, chronic CSR, posterior uveitis.
points: Fluorescence weak (1/25 of fluorescein) → video/SLO capture. Dose 25–50 mg; images up to ~45 min.
Phases: early (<1 min), early mid (1–3), late mid (3–15), late (15–45).
Better tolerated; anaphylaxis similar. Contains iodide → avoid with iodine allergy (iodine-free versions exist). Relative CI: liver disease, pregnancy unknown.
Hyper: window, leakage, abnormal vessels. Hypo: blockage; PED looks dark on ICGA (bright on FA); choriocapillaris non-perfusion = geographic dark areas; stromal foci = even dark dots.
Uses: PCV (polyps), AMD adjunct, RAP (hot spot), chronic CSR (dilated leaky choroidal vessels), posterior uveitis, tumours, lacquer cracks/angioid streaks, when FA contraindicated.
chunks.hook: ICGA = choroid's camera. PED: bright on FA, dark on ICGA.

cards.q: Condition for which ICGA is far superior to FA?
cards.a: Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy.

cards.q: How does a PED appear on ICGA vs FA?
cards.a: Hypofluorescent on ICGA; hyperfluorescent (pooling) on FA.

chunks.title: OCT & OCT-angiography
chunks.tldr: OCT = 'ultrasound with light': cross-section of retinal layers. OCTA shows flow without dye, but no leakage (and misses very slow/fast flow).
points: Near-infrared interferometry. Spectral/Fourier domain (fast, high resolution); swept-source (deeper, faster).
Layers: NFL, GCL, IPL, INL, OPL, ONL, ELM, ellipsoid zone (IS/OS), outer segments, RPE, choriocapillaris.
Thickness maps, 3D. Revolutionised AMD, DMO, holes, ERM, VMT, CSR, RVO. Distinguishes RD vs retinoschisis.
OCTA: repeated B-scans detect moving red cells → flow maps by layer.
OCTA uses: CNV (incl. non-exudative CNV in dry AMD), DR (NV vs IRMA, ischaemia, deep plexus), MacTel, PCV, chronic CSR, tumours.
Limits: no leakage/pooling/staining; flow outside the detection range missed.
chunks.hook: OCTA shows the pipes with water running — not the leaks.

cards.q: Main limitation of OCT-angiography compared with FA?
cards.a: It doesn't show leakage, pooling or staining.

chunks.title: Autofluorescence & wide-field
chunks.tldr: FAF shows lipofuscin in RPE without dye. In GA, a bright (hyper-AF) rim at the edge predicts where atrophy spreads next. Dark = dead/stressed RPE.
points: Shows more disease than visible clinically.
GA: hyper-AF leading edge comes before the cells die.
Wide-field: one shot of ~80% of the retina (~200°), often undilated; can do FA/FAF too.
Zones: posterior pole (within arcades) → mid-periphery (to vortex ampullae) → far periphery (anterior to ampullae).
chunks.hook: Bright rim = next to go.

cards.q: What does a hyperautofluorescent rim around geographic atrophy suggest?
cards.a: Stressed RPE that is likely to atrophy next (lesion growth).

chunks.title: AMD: classification & risk factors
chunks.tldr: Dry ~90% (end-stage = geographic atrophy); wet ~10% but fast severe loss. Classify by drusen within 2 DD of fovea: <63 µm normal ageing, 63–125 early, >125 or pigment intermediate, GA/CNV late.
points: Most common cause of irreversible blindness in industrialised countries.
Late AMD in one eye → ~50% fellow eye within 5 yrs.
Risk: age (biggest), white race, family history (3×), smoking (2×), hypertension/CVS, high-fat diet/obesity, ?aspirin (wet).
Genes: CFH (1q31, complement; 7× homozygous) and ARMS2 (10q26; 8×). Genetic testing not recommended yet.
Ruler: a retinal vein at the disc edge ≈ 125 µm.
Wet forms: CNV, PED, RAP, PCV.

head: Category
Findings
rows: Large drusen >125 µm or pigment change

chunks.hook: 63 and 125 = 'half a vein, one vein'.

cards.q: Two major AMD susceptibility genes?
cards.a: CFH (complement factor H) and ARMS2.

cards.q: Drusen size defining intermediate AMD?
cards.a: Large drusen >125 µm (or any AMD pigmentary abnormality).

chunks.title: Drusen
chunks.tldr: Drusen = deposits between RPE and Bruch. Bigger + pigment = higher risk. Large drusen both eyes: 13% late AMD in 5 yrs → ~50% if bilateral pigment too.
points: Small/hard (≤63 µm): well-defined; little risk alone.
Intermediate (63–125 µm): small risk; >10% if bilateral pigment.
Large/soft (>125 µm): fuzzy edges, can coalesce → drusenoid PED.
OCT: hyper-reflective lumps under the RPE.
FA: window defect or late staining; lipid-rich drusen stay dark.
Mimics: Doyne honeycomb (radial, AD, young), cuticular drusen (young adults, 'stars in the sky' on FA, CFH), type 2 membranoproliferative GN.
chunks.hook: Cuticular drusen = 'stars in the sky'.

cards.q: FA appearance of cuticular (basal laminar) drusen?
cards.a: Numerous tiny hyperfluorescent dots – 'stars in the sky'.

chunks.title: AREDS supplements
chunks.tldr: Give AREDS2 vitamins for extensive intermediate drusen, ≥1 large druse, GA, or late AMD in one eye. ~25% less progression. Not for early/no AMD.
points: AREDS2 formula: Vit C 500 mg, Vit E 400 IU, lutein 10 mg, zeaxanthin 2 mg, zinc 25–80 mg, copper 2 mg.
Beta-carotene removed → raises lung cancer risk in smokers/ex-smokers.
Lutein/zeaxanthin = safe and probably better.
Omega-3 added nothing. Lower zinc dose works as well, fewer side effects.
Also: stop smoking, green leafy veg, sun protection, oily fish.
chunks.hook: AREDS2: swap beta-carotene → lutein/zeaxanthin; fish oil flopped.

cards.q: Why was beta-carotene removed in AREDS2?
cards.a: Increased lung cancer risk in current/former smokers.

cards.q: Did omega-3 help in AREDS2?
cards.a: No added benefit.

chunks.title: Dry AMD & geographic atrophy
chunks.tldr: Slow, bilateral (asymmetric) loss; better in bright light. Drusen → pigment change → sharp atrophic patches (GA) showing choroidal vessels. FA: window defect. No proven drug yet.
points: Drusen often disappear inside GA.
OCT: RPE + photoreceptor loss, outer retinal tubulations (round dark spaces at GA edge).
Basal laminar deposit (between RPE and its BM) vs basal linear deposit (RPE BM ↔ inner collagen → drusen).
Manage: AREDS if criteria met, risk factors, Amsler grid at home, low vision aids, sight-impaired registration.
Experimental: intraocular telescope, visual cycle modulators. Lampalizumab failed. Laser to drusen doesn't stop progression.
chunks.hook: GA = see-through floor → choroid shows → window defect.

cards.q: What are outer retinal tubulations?
cards.a: Round hyporeflective OCT spaces of degenerating photoreceptors, often at GA margins.

chunks.title: PEDs: serous, fibrovascular, drusenoid, haemorrhagic
chunks.tldr: RPE lifts off Bruch. Serous: orange dome, FA brighter-not-bigger, ICGA dark. Fibrovascular = occult CNV. Drusenoid: from confluent drusen, best outlook. Haemorrhagic: almost always CNV or PCV.
points: Cause: thick Bruch blocks fluid flow from RPE to choroid.
Serous: sharp orange dome. FA pooling; a notch hints CNV. ICGA dark with bright ring. OCT optically empty. No drusen → think PCV.
Serous course: atrophy, RPE tear, CNV in ~⅓ by 2 yrs. Rx: observe if stable; anti-VEGF (5–20% RPE tear risk).
Fibrovascular: irregular, stippled FA leakage. Treat as CNV.
Drusenoid: pale scalloped edges, OCT solid (hyper-reflective), usually no SRF. Observe.
Haemorrhagic: dark red dome, sudden loss; FA blocks.
chunks.hook: Serous = empty balloon; drusenoid = stuffed pillow.

cards.q: Haemorrhagic PED without drusen – think of?
cards.a: Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy.

cards.q: Risk of RPE tear after anti-VEGF for serous PED?
cards.a: About 5–20%.

chunks.title: RPE tear
chunks.tldr: RPE rips at the edge of a PED (spontaneous or after injection/PDT/laser) and scrolls toward the CNV. Bare area = bright; rolled flap = dark.
points: Risk: older, long-standing, large PED with small CNV, RPE wrinkles on OCT.
Sudden visual drop if fovea involved.
Signs: pale crescent (bare) next to dark rolled flap.
FA: flap hypo; bare zone hyper; sharp border.
Poor if subfoveal; fine if fovea spared.
chunks.hook: Rolled carpet: bare floor bright, rolled carpet dark.

cards.q: On which side of the CNV does an RPE tear form?
cards.a: The opposite side; the flap retracts toward the CNV.

chunks.title: CNV: signs, FA & OCT types
chunks.tldr: New choroidal vessels through Bruch. Type 1 = occult (80%, under RPE, PED on OCT). Type 2 = classic (20%, above RPE, early lacy fill, leaks). Type 3 = RAP.
points: Symptoms: subacute painless blur + metamorphopsia.
Signs: grey-green/pink lesion, SRF, CMO, lipid, blood, PED, eventually disciform scar.
Driver: VEGF; inhibitors PEDF, CFH.
FA now: confirm before anti-VEGF, look for PCV/RAP. Monitoring = OCT.
Classic: lacy early → leaks over 1–2 min → late staining. Extrafoveal = ≥200 µm from FAZ centre.
Occult: ill-defined; fibrovascular PED or 'late leakage of undetermined source'.
Predominantly classic = >50% classic; minimally classic = <50%.
ICGA: 'hot spot' or 'plaque'.
chunks.hook: Type 1 = basement (under RPE). Type 2 = 2nd floor (above RPE).

cards.q: FA appearance of classic CNV?
cards.a: Well-defined lacy hyperfluorescence early, progressive leakage, late staining.

cards.q: Where is type 1 CNV on OCT?
cards.a: Between Bruch and the RPE (sub-RPE) – appears as a PED.

chunks.title: Anti-VEGF drugs & trials
chunks.tldr: Anti-VEGF is first line for active CNV; start within 2–3 weeks. Better starting VA = better final VA. Drugs: ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept, brolucizumab.
points: Active = fluid, blood, FA leak, growth, falling VA. Useless on a dry fibrotic scar.
Ranibizumab 0.5 mg: antibody fragment, all VEGF-A. ~95% keep vision, ~⅓ gain 15 letters.
Bevacizumab 1.25 mg: full antibody, off-label, cheap, similar efficacy.
Aflibercept 2 mg: fusion protein binds VEGF-A, VEGF-B, PlGF; 3 loading then every 2 months.
Brolucizumab: tiny molecule, ~half manage 3-monthly (HAWK/HARRIER).
Regimens: monthly, PRN (VA/OCT-guided), treat-and-extend.
Risks: endophthalmitis, RD, lens damage, RPE tear, IOP rise, uveitis; ?stroke.
chunks.hook: VIEW: aflibercept, a view every 2 months. CATT fight: Avastin ≈ Lucentis.

cards.q: Which trials compared bevacizumab with ranibizumab?
cards.a: CATT (and IVAN in the UK) – no significant difference in vision.

cards.q: What does aflibercept bind?
cards.a: VEGF-A, VEGF-B and placental growth factor.

chunks.title: Intravitreal injection, PDT & big bleeds
chunks.tldr: Inject 3.5–4 mm behind limbus (pars plana), povidone-iodine 5% ≥3 min, 30G, 0.05 ml, avoid 3 & 9 o'clock. Check CRA perfusion after. PDT (verteporfin) now rare.
points: Consent, mark eye, mask, topical anaesthetic, speculum; inferotemporal usually.
Chlorhexidine if iodine allergy. No routine post-op antibiotics (resistance).
After: check vision/IOP; CRA occluded by IOP → paracentesis.
Both eyes same day: separate instruments + drug batches.
PDT: IV verteporfin + diode laser → thrombosis. Now for PCV combo, refusing injections, CSR (reduced dose).
Thermal laser only for small extrafoveal classic CNV.
Massive submacular bleed: anti-VEGF + tPA ± pneumatic displacement; review warfarin; think PCV or macroaneurysm.
chunks.hook: After injecting, ask: can they count fingers? (CRA perfused)

cards.q: Distance from limbus for intravitreal injection?
cards.a: 3.5–4.0 mm (pars plana).

cards.q: Management of large submacular haemorrhage?
cards.a: Anti-VEGF + intravitreal/subretinal tPA ± pneumatic displacement.

chunks.title: RAP (type 3 neovascularization)
chunks.tldr: New vessels start inside the retina (deep capillary plexus) and dive down to join the choroid. Bilateral, multiple small superficial haemorrhages, PED. ICGA hot spot.
points: 10–20% of wet AMD in white people.
Stage 1 intraretinal NV → 2 subretinal NV (± serous PED) → 3 CNV with retinal–choroidal anastomosis.
ICGA: hot spot; feeding arteriole + draining venule = 'hairpin loop'.
FA looks like occult/minimally classic.
Rx: anti-VEGF (± PDT).
chunks.hook: RAP = top-down (retina → choroid); CNV = bottom-up.

cards.q: Where does RAP originate?
cards.a: In the retina (deep capillary plexus), later anastomosing with the choroid.

chunks.title: Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV)
chunks.tldr: Pachychoroid disease: branching choroidal network with orange-red polyps. Asian/African, women (5:1), no drusen, big bleeds. Diagnose with ICGA; treat with anti-VEGF + PDT (EVEREST II).
points: Peripapillary or macular orange nodules; recurrent serosanguineous detachments.
Up to 50% settle on their own.
ICGA: early bright nodules + network, leak later. Grape-like clusters = worse.
OCT: 'double-hump', 'inverted V' PED, thick choroid.
Anti-VEGF alone less effective; combo with PDT better (more regression, fewer injections).
AMD not responding to anti-VEGF after 3 months → do ICGA for PCV.
chunks.hook: PCV = Polyps, Pachychoroid, PDT combo.

cards.q: Key investigation for PCV?
cards.a: ICGA.

cards.q: OCT signs of PCV?
cards.a: 'Inverted V' PED, double-hump sign, thick choroid.

chunks.title: PEHCR & idiopathic CNV
chunks.tldr: PEHCR: older women, peripheral haemorrhage + exudate + PED. Idiopathic CNV: <50 yrs, unilateral, diagnosis of exclusion, better prognosis.
points: PEHCR: bilateral in a minority; vision often good; may be an AMD/PCV variant; anti-VEGF if sight-threatening.
Idiopathic CNV: exclude angioid streaks, high myopia, inflammation (e.g. presumed ocular histoplasmosis).
Both treated with anti-VEGF when needed.
chunks.hook: Peripheral blood in an older woman → think PEHCR.

cards.q: Idiopathic CNV – typical patient?
cards.a: Under 50, unilateral, after excluding myopia, angioid streaks and inflammation.

chunks.title: Epiretinal membrane (ERM)
chunks.tldr: Clear fibrocellular sheet on the retina that contracts → wrinkling + distortion. Idiopathic (age, PVD) or secondary (RD surgery commonest). Early 'cellophane' → later 'macular pucker'. Rx: vitrectomy + peel.
points: Idiopathic: glial cells from vitreous remnants after PVD; ~10% bilateral; milder.
Secondary: RD surgery, PRP, cryo, vascular disease, inflammation, trauma; more pigment cells.
Symptoms: blur, metamorphopsia (often none if mild).
Signs: sheen (best in red-free), vessel tortuosity, striae, pseudohole, CMO.
OCT: bright surface layer + thickening; broken IS/OS = worse post-op result.
Surgery: ≥2 lines gain in ~75%, mainly less distortion; slow recovery over months; recurrence rare. ILM peel controversial.
chunks.hook: Cling film on the retina: shrinks → wrinkles.

cards.q: Most common cause of secondary ERM?
cards.a: Retinal detachment surgery.

cards.q: Main benefit of ERM peel?
cards.a: Reduced metamorphopsia (VA improves ≥2 lines in ~75%).

chunks.title: Macular hole: stages
chunks.tldr: Women 60–70; fellow eye ~10% at 5 yrs. Gass: 1a yellow spot → 1b yellow ring → 2 <400 µm → 3 >400 µm + cuff → 4 + complete PVD (Weiss ring).
points: Stage 0 = VMA (OCT only).
1a impending: flat fovea + yellow spot (inner retina pulls off). DDx: vitelliform, solar, CMO.
1b occult: yellow ring.
2: small full-thickness <400 µm, vitreous still attached to the lid.
3: >400 µm, red base, yellow dots, grey cuff of SRF, ± operculum; VA ~6/60.
4: same as 3 + complete PVD.
IVTS size: small ≤250, medium 250–400, large >400 µm.
Microhole <150 µm: mild symptoms, often heals → tiny IS/OS defect.
chunks.hook: Spot → Ring → Small → Big → Big + free vitreous.

cards.q: Gass stage 3 vs 4 macular hole difference?
cards.a: Stage 4 has a complete PVD; clinically otherwise identical.

cards.q: Size cut-off between Gass stage 2 and 3?

chunks.title: Macular hole: tests & treatment
chunks.tldr: Watzke–Allen: slit beam looks broken. OCT diagnoses and stages. Surgery = vitrectomy + ILM peel + gas; closure ~100%, ≥6/12 in ~65%.
points: Amsler: distortion more than scotoma.
FA: early window defect (not needed routinely). FAF: bright foveal spot in stages 3–4.
~50% stage 1 resolve; ~10% FTMH close spontaneously (small ones more).
Ocriplasmin for small early holes with VMT.
Surgery for stage ≥2: better if small and <6 months. Long face-down posturing no longer needed.
Vision improves over months in 80–90%; worse in up to 10%.
chunks.hook: Watzke–Allen: hole = broken line; other disease = bent line.

cards.q: What does a patient with a FTMH report on the Watzke–Allen test?
cards.a: The slit beam is broken or thinned in the centre.

cards.q: Three steps of macular hole surgery?
cards.a: Vitrectomy (relieve traction), ILM peel, gas tamponade.

chunks.title: VMA, VMT, lamellar hole & pseudohole
chunks.tldr: VMA: vitreous stuck within 3 mm, no retinal change. VMT: stuck with retinal distortion. Focal ≤1500 µm, broad >1500 µm. Lamellar hole = partial-thickness; pseudohole = ERM edges heaped up, no tissue lost.
points: Anomalous PVD = gel stays stuck at the macula.
VMT concurrent (with AMD/RVO/DR) or isolated.
VMT symptoms: blur, distortion, photopsia, micropsia. VMA: none.
Lamellar hole: inner retina defect, photoreceptors intact; classic sequel of CMO.
OCT is key.
Rx: observe (often releases); ocriplasmin releases VMT in ~25% (worse if ERM; rare diffuse retinal dysfunction); vitrectomy usually works.
chunks.hook: VMA = Attached, fine. VMT = Tugging, trouble.

cards.q: Difference between VMA and VMT?
cards.a: VMT has retinal structural changes/distortion on OCT; VMA does not.

cards.q: What is ocriplasmin?
cards.a: Recombinant plasmin injected intravitreally to release vitreomacular traction.

chunks.title: Central serous chorioretinopathy
chunks.tldr: Young/middle-aged man (3:1), steroids, stress → serous bubble under the macula from leaky RPE. VA improves with plus lens. FA ink blot or smokestack. ~80% resolve in 3–6 months.
points: Risks: any steroid (incl. Cushing), pregnancy, H. pylori, hypertension, sleep apnoea, dialysis, stress.
Symptoms: unilateral blur, distortion, micropsia, mild colour loss; VA ~6/9–6/18.
Signs: round serous detachment, small PEDs, old RPE scars; chronic → gravitational tracts (FAF). Check for optic pit.
Recurrence up to 50%; chronic (>12 months) ~15% → permanent loss.
OCT: empty neurosensory dome, thick choroid. ICGA: dilated, hyperpermeable choroid.
FA: ink blot (common) or smokestack (column).
Rx: observe, stop steroids; spironolactone; half-dose/fluence PDT for chronic; micropulse laser; eplerenone (limited evidence).
chunks.hook: Stressed man on steroids, plus lens helps → CSR. Smoke rises from the stack.

cards.q: Two FA patterns of CSR?
cards.a: Ink blot (common) and smokestack.

cards.q: Treatment for chronic CSR?
cards.a: Half-dose/half-fluence verteporfin PDT (also micropulse laser; stop steroids).

chunks.title: Macular telangiectasia (MacTel)
chunks.tldr: Type 1: unilateral, middle-aged men, aneurysms + exudate (Coats cousin). Type 2: bilateral, commoner, temporal parafoveal greying, crystals, right-angle venules, Müller cell loss, no exudate.
points: Type 1: telangiectasia, microaneurysms, CMO, lipid ring. Rx: laser to leaks, anti-VEGF.
Type 2: equal sex, mid-life; loss of foveal reflex; grey parafoveal retina; superficial crystals; RPE plaques.
Type 2 OCT: inner retinal cavities (not CMO), IS/OS loss. FA: leakage but no petaloid CMO.
Type 2 MPOD: oval loss of macular pigment (≈ pathognomonic).
Type 2 proliferative stage: subretinal NV (RAP-like); anti-VEGF helps there.
VA rarely <6/60 unless CNV.
Type 3: occlusive, very rare, poor prognosis.
chunks.hook: Type 1 = 1 eye, aneurysms. Type 2 = 2 eyes, grey + crystals + right angles.

cards.q: Typical vessel sign in MacTel type 2?
cards.a: Blunted dilated venules turning at right angles into the deep retina.

cards.q: Which MacTel type resembles Coats disease?
cards.a: Type 1 (aneurysmal telangiectasia).

chunks.title: Cystoid macular oedema
chunks.tldr: Fluid in OPL + INL cysts. FA: petaloid (flower petal). OCT: cysts + lost foveal dip. Causes: surgery, DR/RVO, uveitis, prostaglandin drops, RP, ERM, CNV.
points: Starts in Müller cells; cysts merge → lamellar hole.
Also: tumours (capillary haemangioma), renal failure.
Signs: lost foveal reflex, honeycomb cysts (red-free + contact lens), ± disc swelling.
Microcystic macular oedema: INL microcysts in optic neuropathy (retrograde degeneration) – not classic CMO.
chunks.hook: CMO = flower petals on FA.

cards.q: Which retinal layers contain fluid in CMO?
cards.a: Outer plexiform (Henle) and inner nuclear layers.

chunks.title: Degenerative (pathological) myopia
chunks.tldr: High myopia = >−6 D / AL >26 mm. Signs: tigroid fundus, tilted disc + crescent, lacquer cracks, coin haemorrhages, Fuchs spot, staphyloma. CNV in 10% → anti-VEGF. Kids: atropine 0.01% + outdoors.
points: Atropine 0.01% at night for ages 5–15 progressing >1 D/yr.
Lacquer cracks: breaks in RPE–Bruch–choriocapillaris (~5%) → CNV risk.
Coin haemorrhage: from lacquer crack, no CNV needed.
Fuchs spot: raised pigmented scar after a bleed.
Staphyloma (~⅓): linked to macular hole, dome-shaped macula.
Intrachoroidal cavitation: yellow-orange area inferior to disc; field loss mimics glaucoma.
Myopic CNV: better prognosis than AMD, fewer injections (higher RD risk).
Foveoschisis / macular hole → RD. Others: RRD, lattice, PSC/early nuclear cataract, POAG/pigmentary/steroid response, lens dislocation.
Syndromes: Stickler, Marfan, Down, Ehlers–Danlos, prematurity, Noonan, Pierre Robin.
chunks.hook: Myopic maculopathy: Cracks → Coins → Fuchs.

cards.q: What is a Fuchs spot?
cards.a: Raised pigmented macular lesion after absorption of a subretinal haemorrhage in high myopia.

cards.q: Atropine for myopia control: dose?
cards.a: 0.01% nightly.

chunks.title: Angioid streaks
chunks.tldr: Cracks in brittle, calcified Bruch radiating from the disc. Causes: PXE (most common), Paget, sickle/haemoglobinopathies. Main threat: CNV.
points: ~50% have a systemic link. PXE = 'plucked chicken' neck skin (Grönblad–Strandberg).
Paget ~2%; haemoglobinopathies via iron in Bruch. Probably no real link with Ehlers–Danlos.
Signs: grey/red serrated lines ringing the disc, peau d'orange, disc drusen (up to 25%).
>70% eventually lose vision: CNV, choroidal rupture after minor trauma, foveal streak.
Avoid scleral indentation; protective glasses, no contact sports.
FA window defects; FAF shows more streaks than seen. CNV → anti-VEGF (often recurs).
chunks.hook: PPS: PXE, Paget, Sickle — cracked like old plaster.

cards.q: Most common systemic association of angioid streaks?
cards.a: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum.

cards.q: Most common cause of visual loss in angioid streaks?
cards.a: CNV.

chunks.title: Choroidal folds & hypotony maculopathy
chunks.tldr: Choroidal folds: horizontal stripes; crest yellow/bright on FA, trough dark. Exclude raised ICP, orbital mass, thyroid, scleritis. Hypotony (IOP <6): radiating retinal folds + CMO, often after trabeculectomy with antimetabolites.
points: Idiopathic folds in hypermetropes; acquired hypermetropia + folds → check ICP even without papilloedema.
Other causes: retrobulbar tumour, choroidal tumour, buckle, hypotony.
OCT tells choroidal vs retinal folds (retinal = ERM).
Imaging: B-scan, CT/MRI (enlarged optic nerve sheath).
Hypotony causes: over-filtration, wound leak, cyclodialysis cleft, uveitis/cyclitic membrane, RD; systemic: dehydration, DKA, uraemia, CAIs.
Hypotony signs: shallow AC, choroidal effusion, disc oedema. UBM for cleft. Fix IOP early → better recovery.
chunks.hook: Folds + new hyperopia → think pressure behind the eye.

cards.q: FA of choroidal folds?
cards.a: Hyperfluorescent crests (thinned RPE) and hypofluorescent troughs.

cards.q: Hypotony is defined as IOP below?
cards.a: 6 mmHg.

chunks.title: Solar retinopathy, FCE & dome-shaped macula
chunks.tldr: Solar: eclipse viewing → small yellow foveal spot → tiny foveal defect; usually recovers in 6 months. FCE: choroidal dip on OCT. Dome-shaped macula: myopes, bulge seen on vertical/horizontal OCT, anti-VEGF useless.
points: Solar: photochemical; small central scotoma within hours; OCT outer retinal hole. No treatment. Mimic: laser pointer.
FCE: middle-aged, East Asian; conforming vs non-conforming; complications CNV, CSR, PCV.
Dome-shaped macula: may be a localised staphyloma; serous detachment; ~25% fluid clears; vision usually stable.
chunks.hook: Sun-gazer = pinhole burn at the fovea.

cards.q: Does anti-VEGF help dome-shaped macula SRF?
cards.a: No.

chunks.title: Low vision aids
chunks.tldr: Everything = magnification + good light. Five types: non-optical, tints/filters, convex magnifiers, telescopes, electronic.
points: Non-optical: large print, talking clocks, liquid level indicators.
Tints: grey cut glare; yellow boosts contrast; anti-reflective coating.
Hand magnifiers (best with light); spectacle/dome magnifiers free both hands but fixed distance.
Telescopes: distance to near, but small shallow field.
Electronic/CCTV: 1.5–45×, expensive.
chunks.hook: 'No Tiny Magnifier Too Expensive' = Non-optical, Tints, Magnifiers, Telescopes, Electronic.

cards.q: Main drawback of telescopic low vision aids?
cards.a: Small, shallow visual field.
